a: The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is the largest and most powerful space telescope ever built, designed primarily to observe the universe in infrared wavelengths. Unlike the Hubble Space Telescope, which observes mainly in visible and ultraviolet light, JWST is optimized for infrared because the light from the earliest stars and galaxies has been stretched by the expansion of the universe into longer infrared wavelengths. Additionally, infrared can penetrate dust clouds that block visible light, allowing JWST to see star-forming regions and planetary systems that Hubble cannot. JWST's key technological marvel is its 6.5-meter primary mirror, composed of 18 hexagonal beryllium segments coated in gold. Gold is an excellent reflector of infrared light. The mirror segments can be precisely aligned after launch using tiny actuators. JWST operates from the Sun-Earth L2 Lagrange point, about 1.5 million kilometers from Earth, where it maintains a stable orbit while staying aligned with Earth's orbit around the Sun. This position keeps the Sun, Earth, and Moon all on the same side of the telescope. To detect faint infrared signals from across the cosmos, JWST must be kept extremely cold — below 50 Kelvin (-223°C). A five-layer, tennis-court-sized sunshield blocks heat from the Sun, Earth, and Moon, allowing the telescope and instruments to passively cool to their operating temperatures. JWST carries four scientific instruments: NIRCam (near-infrared camera), NIRSpec (near-infrared spectrograph), MIRI (mid-infrared instrument), and FGS/NIRISS (fine guidance sensor and near-infrared imager and slitless spectrograph). These instruments can capture images, split light into spectra for chemical analysis, and precisely point the telescope. By peering back over 13.5 billion years, JWST allows astronomers to study the first galaxies that formed after the Big Bang, the birth of stars and planetary systems, and the atmospheres of exoplanets.
